clips.title: They Took Away 90% of This National Monument. Now What?

caption_lines.text: So, in recent news, two of our national
monuments, Grand Staircase-Escalante
and Bears Ears that are located here in
Utah where I live, they have been in the
hot seat with boundaries of the
monuments being reduced. So, as someone,
me, who cares deeply about protecting
our public lands, I have been wanting to
get a lot closer to the source to try to
understand
what it actually means to be involved in
public land protection and what
nonprofit organizations that work to
protect public lands actually do. So,
today, I've got Jackie Grant, who is the
executive director of Grand
Staircase-Escalante
Partners, and she's joining me to have
this discussion. So, Jackie, thanks for
being here. I'm excited to to talk about
public lands. I'm excited to
dig into nonprofits, understand it
better, and just have an hour of
education, basically.
>> All right, fantastic, Devon. Really nice
to meet you.
>> Yeah. So, I think it makes the most
sense, since we're talking about Grand
Staircase as kind of the the topic here
and national monuments,
what does Grand Staircase-Escalante
Partners do as an organization to like,
I don't know, set the stage for
understanding nonprofits and the mission
and all of that?
>> Sure, sure. Grand Staircase-Escalante
Partners is a nonprofit that serves the
Grand Staircase-Escalante National
Monument and the public lands that are
connected to the monument as well as the
watersheds that are connected to this
area. And as you know, Grand Staircase
is surrounded by national parks, it's
surrounded by forest service lands, and
private lands as well. And all of these
together create this giant community of
public lands that is really important to
protect. So,
our mission is to serve these public
lands with the Grand Staircase being the
heart of the area that we serve. And we
use tools
uh in restoration, science, stewardship,
and outreach to improve the
on-the-ground conditions on the monument
and on these public lands. And to build
community among the people who love
America's public lands.
>> Cool. Cool.
Would you get into maybe some more
detail of like some of that stewardship
work that's done? Cuz I think that is
something that maybe
I I didn't understand for a long time of
what a nonprofit does cuz I feel like we
we say, "Okay, we we work to protect
public lands. We want like to be
involved in that protection, use your
voices, and vote, and all of those
things."
But I think that there's a lot that goes
on
that maybe doesn't get seen as much and
and and and can have like a big effect
on
your desire as somebody that loves to
recreate to get involved if that if that
makes sense. So, like
>> Yeah.
>> What what are some of the the
stewardship things cuz you talked about
like
the on-the-ground aspects. What was the
Grand Staircase Partners doing in that
regard?
>> Sure thing. So, we have three major
programs. One is stewardship, and that
program is spe-
specifically focused on cleaning up and
mitigating visitor impacts. So, if
you've ever been to a campsite that
looks like perhaps in the past it had 15
separate campfire rings, that half of
which were a big mess.
Our group comes in, we tidy up the spot,
maybe we set aside three campfire rings
that are in really good condition, and
then we clean up all that charcoal, so
it doesn't get all over your gear and
your stuff while you're hanging out
after a long day of canyoning or hiking
or whatever it was you happen to be
doing out on the monument.
That same team also picks up trash.
We pick up human waste, even though I'm
the executive director, I have been out
with that team and I have shoveled up
human waste on the national monument,
because nobody wants to camp in that,
and there aren't a lot of public
restrooms out on the national monument.
That team also picks up
um
non-native plants. So, if you've ever
ridden your bike over a goat head, we
have a day where we go out and we haul
out goat heads, so that people don't
have that terrible experience of having
their tires punctured by these nasty
seeds.
We have a restoration program, and they
steward the land by removing Russian
olives out of the Escalante River
watershed.
And if you've followed the history of
Russian olives over time, they are
non-native tree, they were introduced
for erosion control, and they actually
did too good of a job, and they started
clogging up the rivers.
Right? [laughter] Kind of how it goes,
you know? This looks like it's going to
be really good for solving problem X,
and then it solves and contributes to
problems X, Y, and Z, and then double A,
B, C, you know, so on and so forth.
So, that team works on removing those
Russian olives, and they also focus a
lot on low-tech process-based
restoration, which is a nerdy way of
saying we build really small dams and uh
erosion control structures out of wood,
dirt, and rocks in the national monument
and in other public lands. And these
really tiny erosion control structures,
you know, some are only 3 to 4 ft
across, help slow down the water after
say a wildfire when we have out of
control floodwaters and no vegetation in
place to hold them there.
So, they do that work and even though
it's tiny, it can have a big effect on
preserving the environment after a
wildfire, after the monsoon season, if
we install enough structures on the
ground.
And then the third program that we have
is our native plant program, which is a
really new program for us. It's just in
its second year. And in that program, we
work with the National Seeds of Success
program.
And we collect seeds from native plants
to use in restoration after wildfire and
other disturbances on the ground like
flooding, like oil and gas development.
Whatever the disturbance is, our seeds
can eventually be used to restore that
landscape so it's not just soil anymore
or dirt or rocks. It is the plants that
are meant to live in that environment.
So, we collect
only 20%. We want to make sure that our
native plant populations can grow year
after year.
So, we have a whole protocol in place to
make sure that we only collect what the
population can sustain. And then some of
those seeds go into a national seed bank
where they're stored for future use.
Some go to local farmers where the
farmers will grow them out into the
really big numbers that we need to do
large-scale restoration on the
landscape.
>> Cool.
That's
a lot going on. I think way more than
probably a lot of people a lot of people
think about. And I mean, for me, I've
I had actually
uh
I think it was last year
signed up to volunteer for one of the
the trips to go do a clean up of the
main Escalante Canyon uh that halfway
you meet Death Hollow. And I think it
was to
maybe human waste, but also
uh like trash and then and fire rings.
And unfortunately, I had something come
up. I wasn't able to to do it, but like
I was really excited about it because I
work as a guide for Utah Valley

I use that section of trail and the
river as like one of my main trips that
I do. And so I see all the time how much
impact year over year and even like in
the spring, I'll take a group and then
you see the
6 months of time from like March to
September when I take another group, how
much it's changed and the amount of
either trash or impact that you see from
from people that I don't want to like
call anybody out or throw people under
the bus and say they're in
being malicious or intentionally like
causing issue, but
I often see
like charcoal
graffiti on
the the slick rock on the walls and it's
I
I don't know. It's just an interesting
thing to observe, but it's even cooler
to know that there's an organization
that is working to like help handle
that. And not just like
turn it turn it into a trash field or

as if somebody was trying to carve

>> [laughter]
>> Mhm. Mhm. That's a lot of time and
effort, right?
>> Yeah. Yeah, it is.
Okay.
Um I guess moving on,
I I want to kind of focus a little bit
on the monument itself because
you see so much in the news of like this
is happening, Grand Staircase and Bears
Ears have just recently had uh
boundaries reduced in size, and I'm I'm
curious to just get into a little bit of
not necessarily politically what's
what's happening and like choose a side,
but I'm curious to understand better
from your perspective as an
organization, like what makes Grand
Staircase
Escalante unique and like why is access

maybe what has these changes that have
taken place,
what does it actually mean if if that
makes sense?

But to address the first part of your
question of what makes Grand
Staircase-Escalante National Monument so
unique is the fact that it is the size
that it is. Right? So it covers five
separate life zones. Maybe you have
visited the monument and you've been in
the desert. That is one of the life
zones and you had to be prepared for
water and having enough water and
finding shade and keeping cool. Or maybe
you went into the arid shrublands, which
is the next step up in the life zones
that the monument connects. And then you
probably have been into the riparian
canyonlands like we were just talking
about. And then finally there
[clears throat] are the pinyon-juniper
woodlands and the coniferous subalpine
forest. So essentially what we're doing
is going up in elevation
throughout these different life zones,
which have completely different animals
and plants in each one of them. But one
of the reasons that this area is so
unique, the monument, is because all
five life zones are represented, which
means that animals that have amazing
migratory pathways have the ability to
move through the landscape unimpeded and

they do as organisms like elk and deer

You know, all of those large mammals
have a place in the Grand
Staircase-Escalante National Monument.
But you know what else we have? Little
animals migrating like tarantulas and
hummingbirds. It turns out that the
Grand Staircase-Escalante National
Monument is in the heart of the
migration the migratory pathway of the
rufous hummingbird and a few other
hummingbirds as well. And there has been
a really long-term hummingbird study in
the Escalante uh center that is run by
the BLM and a couple other federal
federal agencies. So, just an amazing
place in terms of the life that it
captures and the diversity of landscapes
and animals and plants as well.
>> Got you.
>> And maybe remind me of the next part of
the question cuz that was a lot.

what does the reduction of the monument

we don't really know,

bottom.

that is something known as the

>> Yeah.
>> Um yeah,
yeah.
>> [laughter]
>> I used to be a university professor, so

the the meantime, the other thing that
this decision, which is through a

Um
the new monument boundaries, not only

bikers already know. The rear wheel of a
mountain bike takes a lot more abuse.
So, that front wheel did survive test
number one and the rear didn't. But I
had loads of information and a very
clear demonstration of why airless
mountain bike tires are not sold. And
unless you're a mountain biker, that
reason might not be obvious. You see, my
tires were 3D printed at home on one
material and they were designed by a guy
with no professional engineering
experience. So, let's assume a capable
R&D lab with experienced engineers and
vast resources could fix all the
problems with my design. And let's
assume the end result was a $300 airless
mountain bike tire that performs almost
as well as a pneumatic tire. So, more
expensive and slightly lower
performance, but completely immune to
punctures. This is the same commercially
viable formula for road going airless
tires sold today. And for mountain
bikes, it has mostly been done already.
The energy return wheel was functioning
in 2012. [music] And while it was not
totally done, it was getting there. So,
on the surface, this seems viable. Yet,
an airless mountain bike tire still has
never been sold ever. And that's because
punctures on mountain bike tires are not
a big enough problem to warrant a
trade-off. Most of us are riding
tubeless tires with sealant. A puncture
isn't always the end of your ride. Your
tire may self-heal. And if you are
experiencing punctures, there are tires
with heavier casings. There are rim
protection inserts. The heaviest tire
you can get with an insert filled with
sealant is still slightly lighter than
my airless tire. But it is true that
even the burliest mountain bike tire
with added protection can still go flat.
But now, we're not talking about
punctures. Punctures are the least of
what the hardest riders are worried
about. They are smashing their rims on
square-edged rocks and tearing their
tires to shreds. Sometimes they're
blowing the rim to pieces. There's no
reason to expect that an airless tire
would fare better in the actual
circumstances that cause mountain bike
tires to go flat. So, it's not that a
viable airless mountain bike tire is
impossible to make. It's that the
problem it solves, punctures, isn't that
big of a problem for mountain bikes,
which would totally explain the timing
on the Energy Return Wheel. In 2012,
when these video clips of the Energy
Return Wheel were taken, tubeless
mountain bike tires with sealant were
increasing in popularity and have gained
more traction every year since. Today,
mountain bikes sold at Walmart ready.
So, it's not that big mountain bike tire
is locking these engineers in dungeons
to protect their IP. It's that a
different technology solved the problem
in a lighter, cheaper, and
higher-performing package. But I don't
really care if it's practical. I'm
already working on version two. You can
see in this little section here, I've
smoothed out certain failure points and
even included bottom-out tokens. Best of
all, both the tokens and the tire knobs
are printed on a slightly softer TPU for

But yeah, airless mountain bike tires
will never truly make sense. So, why did

People were interested. And if I can get

clips.title: SRAM's Gearbox Problem

caption_lines.text: So, what's the deal with gearboxes? Why
is it such bad news for SRAM? And why
now? Well, behind me I have a Pinion
gearbox. It's on my Surly Moonlander and
it works much like a derailleur and a
cassette. You shift gears, except it
happens up here inside this little
enclosed box. It's mostly sealed up and
so you only have to maintain it like
once a year. You just change the oil in
it. There are a lot of desirable
features inside a gearbox, but not a lot
of big, big companies have put time and
effort into them for bicycles because
they already have derailleurs and
cassettes. They work very well and the
perception of a gearbox is that it
creates a lot of problems. Yes, it is
heavy. That's real. And then, yes, it
has a little bit of drag in certain
gears. Maybe you wouldn't want it on a
XC race bike. But for a lot of
applications, it's really not that big
of a problem. And it's especially not a
big problem if you pair it with an
e-bike motor because the weight, the
drag, they become pretty much invisible.
And so, that's what we're seeing is a
lot of companies working on e-bike
gearboxes. And it's not just this new
feature that we're going to see. This is
going to disrupt the entire market,
especially the drivetrain market because
companies like SRAM, who have been
working for decades and decades on
drivetrain technology, are going to find
the market that they tried to corner
built into somebody else's motor. Now,
I'll name names in a moment, but I want
you to put a bookmark on this next
point. When you have a gearbox and a
motor together, you have the
electronics, you have the app, you have
the entire ecosystem, replacement
chargers, replacement motors. You have
all these things built into one. And
whoever wins that race is going to take
more than just a new product category.
They're going to take categories that
used to exist for other people away from
them. There are a whole slew of
companies working on motor gearboxes
right now. It's really exciting.
Sometimes it's just a patent, sometimes
they've actually officially announced
they're working on it, and there are
even release dates. There are even motor
gearboxes that are out in the wild right
now, most notably Pinion's MGU. That has
raised Pinion's profile tremendously,
but we still have not seen one of the
really big guys adopt it, and that's
changing right now because Avannatech
released their MG concept at Eurobike
this year, and it's kind of a big deal.
Canyon already is slated to have it on
their bikes, and so we're going to see a
lot of manufacturers adopting this, and
they're going to be taking part of
SRAM's market share right from the rear
of the bike and putting it into the
bottom bracket. But why? Why should this
be such a big concern for SRAM? They
already have relationships with all the
biggest bike companies, and they already
sell them product. They could make their
own gearbox, and they could sell it to
them, right? Well, it's not just a
gearbox, it's a motor gearbox. So, when
you are adopting this product, not only
you're adopting the gearbox, but you're
adopting the motor, the app, the
battery, the software updates, the
entire ecosystem. Clearly Trek and
Specialized understand this. If you want
to get a new motor for your Trek, you
can't just go straight to TQ. It's
software locked. You need to get it from
a Trek dealer. And Specialized is in the
same boat. And then there's the motor
itself. SRAM has tried to bring a motor
to market, SRAM Powertrain. I've tested
it. It's really good. It feels great.
But, not a lot of big companies have
adopted it. Yes, there are a few Propane
Transition. We've seen nowhere near the
adoption of SRAM's traditional
drivetrains, and that's a problem
because now they're going to presumably
use a very similar motor, probably
Brose, which is now owned by Yamaha, and
they're going to sell it with their
gearbox. And so the question is, what
would happen if SRAM produced the best
gearbox on the market? Let's say it was
way better than the one that Avannatech
is working on.
Would they still have the best motor?
And which one would buyers choose? Which
one would they care about? The motor or
the gearbox? My vote is the motor
because we've seen e-bike buyers
actually really care about the motor.
They really care about the battery.
That's what they want, power and range.
And so, if SRAM's gearbox is better, but
then Avinox has a better motor or a more
desirable motor, that's a problem for
SRAM. It's a really big problem for SRAM
and we've seen that companies like
Canyon have already decided which one
they're going to go with. You've seen
people out there with brand new e-bikes.
They clearly ride them all the time.
They're clearly obsessed with it and
they're just in the same gear the entire
time. They're like barely using it. And
so, there are a lot of e-bike buyers
that just don't care about gears at all
because they're not constantly trying to
squeeze the most power out of the bike.
It's just there. They want to get up the
hill so they can go down. That doesn't
describe every e-bike buyer, but clearly
the market is listening. That's why
we're seeing things like automatic
shifting and CVTs, continuously variable
gearboxes like the one that Avinox is
creating. It's there so that you don't
have to think about the shifting. Now,
yeah, I shift gears all the time. You
shift gears all the time, but I'm just
telling you the reality on the ground
right now. The companies are listening
and they know what e-bike buyers want.
So, a motor gearbox simplifies the
assembly in some ways. It makes the bike
more reliable. It takes some of the
thinking out of shifting in many cases
and it also takes one of the most
expensive parts of a bike build, which
is the drivetrain, and puts it all into
one package, which could potentially be
a really compelling value, especially
for a bike company that also has to
assemble the thing and manage
relationships between different
manufacturers. So, it's pretty clear
that at least in terms of e-bikes, the
writing is on the wall. If a company
like Trek or Specialized were to develop
their own gearbox, they could keep
everybody in the same ecosystem they're
already in and they don't have to buy a
drivetrain from SRAM or somebody else.
There's a lot to gain from it. And if
they don't do it, they're not going to
be competitive with companies like
Canyon who are adopting Kindernock's MG.
So, everybody is going to be working on
this and it's going to be taking part of
the e-bike pie from SRAM. But it gets so
much worse. I want to give you a little
bit of context that I learned when I
used to work with Box Components years
ago. They were trying to make their own
derailleur and their own clutch. And the
big problem was they had to dance around
all kinds of patents from SRAM and
Shimano that have been around for years.
And so they had to develop their own
clutch. The clutch on a derailleur is
the part that keeps it from bouncing
around. And they had to just use these
friction plates to try and make the
thing stay put. And no matter how good
an engineer you have, it's hard to get
around a patent. And SRAM and Shimano
have decades and decades of building up
patents. And bringing a gearbox, a motor
gearbox into the equation, just opens
that up for everybody because it's
nowhere near as mature of a market. And
so even if you can think of every single
way that it can be done and file as many
patents as you can, there going to be
blind spots. And that's why we see a
whole list of company making these
things. They're not stepping on each
other's toes like they would with a
derailleur. And that creates another
entry point to the very part of the
market that companies like Box
Components and TRP and everybody else
that's working on drivetrains was trying
to get into for years but couldn't
because of those patents. Human powered
bikes. If you go back to 2015 and you
read an article or watch a YouTube video
about some kind of drivetrain product
that is new, somebody's going to come
into the comments and be like, "Yeah,
big whoop. We didn't get the gearbox
we've been asking for." And yeah, Pinion
kind of gave us that gearbox, but what
they're really implying is that a big
drivetrain maker like SRAM or Shimano
should be pouring millions and millions
of dollars and putting the best
engineers on a gearbox to give us the
gearbox we really wanted, the light
efficient gearbox that closes the gap
between a gearbox and a derailleur. And
now, as a consequence of making motor
gearboxes, we're going to make all
gearboxes for bicycles better. And yeah,
I know there's already technology on
ATVs and motorcycles that's different
than the ones we're going to be putting
on bicycles. Few were really working on
that in a big way except for Pinion. And
now we're talking about the big guys
doing it. We're talking about everybody
pouring millions and millions of dollars
and their best engineers into gearboxes.
We've never seen that before and it's
stepping right on SRAM's toes. It's
going in the side door. Now, up until
now I've mentioned certain facts, things
that are factual, products that are
actually coming out, companies that have
deals, but we haven't ventured into wild
speculation and I'm going to continue
doing that as we talk about Specialized.
They're notoriously secretive, but we
can kind of anticipate what a company
like Specialized is going to do because
currently they have their own motors.
Yes, Brose manufactures some of them. I
think Mahle manufactures some other
ones, but Specialized has their
engineers working on these motors and
developing them. So, they have something
proprietary for their Levo ecosystem,
which of course includes the battery,
the app, the charger, everything and you
have to get it from a Specialized
dealer. There is no way that Specialized
is going to relinquish that ecosystem to
SRAM. Absolutely no way. And as I
mentioned earlier, they're going to have
to have an answer to Avanoq MG, which
their competitors like Canyon,
absolutely a big guy, is going to be
carrying on their flagship bikes. And
so, Specialized is going to need a
gearbox, too. Where are they going to
get it? Well, if I were a betting man, I
would say they're going to make their
own and that might be in partnership
with another manufacturer, maybe Yamaha.
That might sound silly, but actually
Yamaha just bought Brose's entire e-bike
division. And as I mentioned before,
Brose manufactures motors for
Specialized already. Yamaha has like a
half a century experience making
gearboxes, and so maybe they would be a
manufacturing partner, or maybe
Specialized would just bring the entire
thing in-house. I don't know. This is
wild speculation, but we can be pretty
sure they're not going to get it from
SRAM if getting it from SRAM means you
have to adopt their electronics as well.
Now, it's worth noting I haven't
discussed Shimano very much, and there's
a reason for that. Shimano has a very
different strategy than SRAM. SRAM has a
very fast release cycle. They're
constantly innovating and releasing new
products, and that keeps them at the
very top end where they kind of
dominate. Shimano makes big bets over
long time horizons. They make super
reliable stuff that's proven, and their
strength is stability. And so, yeah,
they're definitely going to be working
on a gearbox. Yes, they're definitely
going to be trying to sell it to people,
but I can't tell you what their
long-term strategy is. It's going to be
different from SRAM's, and I think that
SRAM is the most exposed right now.
They're the ones with the most to lose
at this very moment. Now, some of you
have noticed this thing sitting right
next to me, especially the older
audience members know exactly what this
is. This is a Hammerschmidt crankset by
SRAM, which was released in 2008. It was
actually brought to market. It can only
be described as a two-speed gearbox.
This was SRAM's first attempt at a
gearbox, and it went up front. It had
two gears. It had this little shifter up
there, and it was short-lived. So, a
cynic might say, "Well, SRAM should have
seen that through. SRAM should have
perfected this technology, and they'd be
in a very different position right now.
They'd have a first-mover advantage, and
they'd have a gearbox already. The
technology would be mature, and they
could just add a motor to it." But
actually, that's not the case. This was
trying to solve a very different
problem. Bicycles at that time, mountain
bikes, had three speeds up front or two
speeds up front. There was a derailleur
there, too. And SRAM was very
instrumental in completely eliminating
that. And so, the very problem that this
was meant to solve was solved by just
removing it. And then you didn't have
this heavy thing with all this drag.
These were not perfect. And so, the
position SRAM is in right now is very
different. They're actually trying to
replace their own products because they
have no choice. If they want to remain
competitive, they're going to have to.
And that 12-speed motor gearbox that
they are supposedly working on, they are
most definitely working on, and it's
probably going to be really good. And
the motor's probably going to be fine.
E-bike motors will likely follow a
similar trend as smartphone thickness.
Everybody's trying to make their
smartphone thinner and thinner and
thinner. And then eventually it got so
thin that nobody cared anymore. It'll
eventually become something that people
care about less. That's not the problem.
The problem is being the first mover,
the one that's going to get these
relationships with all these companies
and lock them into an ecosystem. And
that's where SRAM is actually not as far
behind as you might think. Semi-credible
rumors suggest that SRAM's gearbox motor
is already out in the wild being tested.
It's been spotted as long as a year ago,
and we're pretty sure that was the thing
in the patent pictures. And so, they are
likely deep in development on this and
already working out the final bugs. And
we know that Avinox MG is unofficially
expected in 2027, and that probably
tracks with SRAM as well. But of course,
we go back to the same problem. This is
a defensive move for SRAM. Best case
scenario, they lose less. And I honestly
don't want to see that happen. Everybody
I've ever talked to from SRAM was an
excellent human being, and I know the
company contributes to World Bicycle
Relief, and they treat their employees
well. And so, I'm not making this video
to prey on SRAM's downfall, but at the
same time, I also want to look out for
you. Is this good for you? And the
answer is probably yes. Competition is
always good for consumers, usually. And
this is creating a lot of competition
for something that was really hard to
compete for before, something that
honestly didn't exist before. And so if
a big company wants to get greedy and
make a product that locks you into some
ecosystem and you have to pay
subscription fees to unlock gears, there
are going to be competitors that can
just eat their lunch. And that's a good
thing, or at least I hope it is. This
video included a lot of wild
speculation, and the gearbox motor
market is much bigger than what I've
discussed. I only mentioned a few
companies, but I hope you had fun
speculating with me today. Thanks for
riding with me today, and I'll see you
next time.

clips.title: WTF Happened at Sturgis?

caption_lines.text: Something happened at the Sturgis
Motorcycle Rally this year and we need
to talk about it. Every single person I
know who attended the Sturgis Motorcycle
Rally this year, 2026, the 86th annual
rally, noticed that attendance was very
low this year. Total transparency, I was
at the rally, but I did not stay in
Sturgis. I actually, for the first time
ever, drove my Pan America in my van and
I camped down in the Keystone area for
10 full days during the rally. So, I
cannot say whether or not I noticed a
big difference in the actual Sturgis
area myself, but I did notice a few key
things that happened this year that I
think we can go ahead and talk about.
So, a lot of people are discussing
online why attendance was low this year.
They say it has everything to do with
price gouging, fuel prices, which was a
big one for me this year. It's too
corporate. The demographic is aging out
or it's just a bad economy year. So, I
think the first thing everyone notices
is the price gouging has gotten quite a
bit out of control. Uh total
transparency, I didn't even buy a
t-shirt this year from Sturgis. I just
didn't feel like I had a very connective
time with it, so I didn't really want to
invest in wearing a shirt from this
year. So, on the subject of shopping, I
think we need to talk about whether or
not this price gouging is actually
affecting people arriving to the rally
or if it's just a byproduct of having
such a large community who want to
attend and deal and vend at the rally.
So, you do kind of have to pay to play,
but at the end of the day, how much do
you pay and is it worth it? So, for me,
I do sell t-shirts. Actually, if you
guys are watching this video right now,
shameless plug, I am soft launching my
brand new Mythic Moto design t-shirts.
I'm phasing out my old t-shirts and I'm
introducing the Burning the Midnight Oil
shirt. This shirt is directly inspired
from my many, many motorcycle trips to
the Sturgis Rally specifically. For
those of you who have to ride thousands
of miles from far away, do multiple Iron
Butts during this experience, and that's
what this shirt is inspired by. So, for
those of you who know the feeling of
solo travel, it's just you and the
stars, and you've been on the road for
15 plus hours, and it's that feeling of
burning the midnight oil. Directly
inspired by
the magic of motorcycling and how we can
do anything we put our minds to to
safely accomplish where we're trying to
go. So, it is a slight reflection of the
rally in general and that vagabond
lifestyle, but yeah, this t-shirt is
available for pre-order only. You cannot
purchase it right now, and I am very
excited to start getting the shirt into
production for you guys because it's
definitely my new favorite design. And
you can head over to mythicmoto.com and
check that out for yourself if you would
like to wear my merchandise. This Again,
this is directly inspired by my
experiences, my art, and my story to
tell. So, yeah, mythicmoto.com
pre-order. Pre-order only. You cannot
purchase it just yet, and pre-order
isn't going to last long. I'll update
you guys about when that ends here in
the future. So, again, the price
gouging, I did not spend too much time
in Sturgis this year. I did head over to
Black Hills Harley-Davidson for a couple
days to see some of my friends who were
vending. Even the vendors, they have to
pay so much money to hopefully sell
their wares, basically. And I completely
understand space is limited,
but I saw a dramatic decrease in people
attending the rally after basically
Wednesday.
Now, we did get some unfavorable
weather, but that is I've never been to
a Sturgis with perfect weather, if I'm
being honest. So, we did get some rain.
There was a really wicked hailstorm that
popped up near Nemo. I was staying in
Keystone, so I got kind of the tail end
of that. And yeah, it was pretty
terrifying and I felt awful for anyone
who was out on a motorcycle experiencing
that. So, I understand why people
probably left halfway through the rally,
but I feel like that's pretty normal,
you know? Again, the rally happened a
week later this year. The Sturgis Rally
starts the first Friday of every August.
So, basically the first Friday of of
this August was a week late and people
were dealing with their work schedules
or kids going back to school or just
their schedules in general of kind of
phasing out of that summertime fun.
Even for me, I was like, "Man, this is
kind of really cutting into some of my
later summer plans that I had going on."
So, I do think a lot of people there was
a mass exodus because they had to get
back home to their families to help put
their kids back in school or what have
you. But then the weather was very
unfavorable. So, imagine being a vendor,
there's a fly in here and it's going to
send me into orbit. So, imagine being a
vendor and paying all this money,
driving across the country with all of
your merchandise, and then basically
losing half of your potential revenue
because the weather went bad. So, I my
heart goes out to those people, but then
also we need to talk about the price
gouging.
I stayed in Deadwood. I camped in
Deadwood in 2025
and there was one night the storm was so
bad. I was truly worried for my safety
that I was going to be struck by
lightning and it was a Monday evening.
So, I looked up at the cheapest hotel I
could find in Deadwood for that Monday
night was almost $600 a night.
So, I let Jesus take the wheel and I
slept in my tent and hoped for the best
and luckily cameraman never dies, but
the price gouging has really
really just I think stopped a lot of
people from even thinking about wanting
to attend. When you are spending a
couple hundred dollars a day when it
comes to just food, drink, fuel, that
really takes the fun
I'm going to get this lie. That really
takes the fun out of wanting to even be
there. Not to mention again,
the Black Hills of South Dakota
are in the middle of a continent
essentially. If you look at the entire
North America, it's right smack in the
middle. So, for most people in the
concentrated areas of the country are
driving well over 1,500 mi to attend
this rally. So, that is time you have to
take off to physically be there. That is
money you have to spend on fuel and
lodging and food just to spend the days
to get to the rally. And we're not in
the best economy right now to be
completely honest. For me personally,
since this was the very first time I
drove a vehicle to the rally, it cost
So, I I I put fuel in my van and then
when I was at the rally, fuel in my
motorcycle. And I only rode around 900
mi during the rally. It cost about $800
just in fuel. That doesn't include
lodging prices. That doesn't include
food. That repairs that I had to make on
the road. I had to buy some things for
my bike to keep it repaired and stuff.
So, it really really adds up. And then
you want people to buy alcohol or buy
merchandise. And all of these vendors
are there sacrificing their time and
energy just staying in one booth hoping
to make a good earnings. And I I
personally just couldn't justify it. I
couldn't justify buying a T-shirt or
buying a new part that I wanted for my
motorcycle because I was already so
outpaced in the fuel and the food and
the stuff I was spending just to be
there. So, the price gouging, I
completely understand
is a huge turn off for a lot of people.
But at the end of the day, it's
something that you budget for and you
plan for.
And I think people are honestly just
tired of it. Not to mention a lot the
lodging and camping and locations that
you can stay at during the rally, the
places that offer the fun things to do
or the meet and greets or the concerts,
you have to pay separately to get into
those places, which again, as a business
owner, I understand you have to pay the
talent that is being there and you need
to make that revenue back. But, I think
that's where a lot of the fun just kind
of gets pulled away from people who have
to sit there and figure out what they're
going to do and what they want to do
during the rally and then actually
justifying the price to get there to pay
for it, getting stuck in traffic or your
bike getting stuck in the mud or you
just There's a lot. I want you guys to
know, I don't feel one particular way or
another about this because for many
people, this is a bucket list trip. This
is their vacation and they are really
ready to pay whatever it takes to have a
good time. Look at people who go to
Disney World. I'm the Sturgis is the
Disney World for motorcyclists,
essentially. And Disney World is so
insanely expensive,
but you're creating lifelong memories
and you know that you have to pay to
play. That's kind of what Sturgis has
turned into and that's not the heart and
soul of what it used to be, but that's
what it is now. And so, I feel like the
creators of the rally and the people who
host it are definitely feeling the pinch
and of how to be bigger and better and
more sustainable for everybody. Um, I
don't personally know what it is. I
don't feel like I'm their target
demographic, but I can tell you my
honest opinions on the things that I
love and the things I can't stand about
the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally. So, one
thing I've been seeing a lot lately is
people saying that it's too corporate
now. You know, you drive down Lazelle,
you ride down Main Street and it's
nothing but billboards, ads, posters,
flyers. It's corporate America. That's
what America was built on was marketing
and advertising. So, all you see is like
Harley-Davidson, Indian, Russ Brown, Law

what am I even
getting out of all of this? And it's
nothing. It's awareness. They just want

what it is. So, the corporateness beside
behind all of these things as I think
where people feel like Sturgis is losing
its soul. Now, as a 37-year-old
millennial, I can't tell you what the
rally used to be. And total
transparency, at the age I am, if I were
to attend the rally back in the '70s and

think I would have been as well received
as I am now just because of the time and

because I've always had this creative

clips.title: Insta360 X6 vs X5 Comparison | WORTH THE UPGRADE?

caption_lines.text: Welcome back to my channel. My name is Jordan Hetrick and I'm the bestselling author of books
about how to use Insta360 cameras, including a book for the X5 and also the brand new Insta360
X6. When these new cameras are released, I always get a lot of questions about what features are
going to make a difference and how the footage compares. So, in this video, I just went out and
I filmed a bunch of beautiful comparisons for you guys so you can look at the footage side
by side and I can help you decide which of these cameras is going to be a better choice for you.
Both of these Insta360 360 cameras are top-notch cameras that are going to give you the best 360
footage. But let me show you some of the features that are different between the two cameras. Now,
let's go take a look at some comparisons between the Insta360 X6 and the Insta360 X5. First,
let's just take a look at the physical differences between these two cameras.
And when I do these comparisons, I'll always put the X6 on the left side of your screen and the
X5 on the right side of the screen just to make it clear for you. So, you can see the two camera
bodies are quite different. The X6 is actually a little bit shorter and a little bit wider.
They're about the same thickness, but they just made it a little more compact, so it's easier
to mount the X6. The X5 screen is a little bit taller and longer, whereas the X6 screen is a
little shorter and more square shaped. And you'll notice on the X6, there's no button at the bottom
of the screen here. You actually have oncreen buttons that are pressure sensitive. So, it's
a little bit different than how the X5 functions. You'll see there's also a physical shutter button
here on the side of the camera. So, if you want to start and stop recording, you can do that there.
As far as weight goes, the X6 is actually a little bit lighter than the X5, but you're not going to
really notice much difference as far as weight goes when you've got it mounted because it's
pretty small. Both of the cameras actually have replaceable lenses, but on the X6, they came out
with kind of a new system for replacing it that's a little bit easier. And also, those replacement
lenses are about half the cost of the X5. Both of the cameras mount basically the same. They have
that quarter-20 in thread on the bottom of the camera here. But the X6 has these little contacts
here. So you can actually use magnetic mounting and mount it to some new accessories like this,
which is a power handle. So now you can actually control the camera through these buttons right
here, even though it's not connected with a cable. So you start and stop recording right there on the
handle. Both of these cameras are waterproof as is without an extra case. So if you want to take
them out in the surf or in a river, you're fine to go in the water with these cameras. However,
when you go underwater, neither of these cameras is going to have sharp videos because those lenses
are curved. to film underwater with either of these cameras. They require a separate dive case,
which is available for both of them, and I'll show you some comparisons between those in just a
minute. In terms of what's on the inside of these two cameras, there's a couple big differences. The
Insta360 X6 has 47 GB of internal storage. So, if you don't have a memory card or you don't want to
use one, you can use that internal storage. The X6 also has new faster processing chips and also
uses dual 1/1.1 in sensors. So, these are going to get you better lowlight footage and also more
detail and quality in your shots. So, you'll be able to take in that low light better and you'll
see this in the comparisons when we go to look at those next. Also, if you haven't subscribed to my
channel yet, be sure to subscribe so that when I come out with new videos for the X6 or the X5,
you can be the first to know about them and learn more about your 360 camera. Now, let's take a look
at some comparisons between what these cameras can create. So, both of these cameras have a few
different recording styles. You can either record 360, full spherical 360 photos and videos, or you
can record flat videos where it's only recording out of one of the lenses at a time. You can also
record gimbal style videos where it can either follow you or follow a subject. Or you can just
use it for gimbal style shots where you've got really smooth footage. First, let's take a look at
some comparisons and 360 video mode because this is going to be the mode that you use most often,
most likely, and it's the most important mode in my opinion. There are a couple things that
I want you to look for as you're watching these comparisons. The first one is the detail in the
shots. With that larger sensor on the X6, when you zoom in on your shots and you crop in, which
is what you need to do when you edit 360 videos, you're going to see more detail in those shots.
So, just look out for that in these comparisons. And also look for the dynamic range. Now, this
isn't necessarily going to make the images look brighter. It's just going to show more detail in
the dark spots and in the bright spots. So, it'll be a better balance in the shots and give you more
balanced images. So in this shot for example, if you look at the sky there, you can really see a
lot more dynamic range. You can see in the clouds it's not so blown out. And that's just because
the X6 has a better dynamic range and can handle those different contrasty lighting conditions.
The X6 has a huge step up in video mode and now records in 8K at 50 frames per second versus 8K
and 30 frames per second on the X5. This basically allows you to film all of your shots, whether you

is really important and having a lot of detail in your shots. So when you zoom in, it still
looks good. In this shot, I'm going to zoom in way beyond where you should zoom in on either of these

I think that's the main thing that Insta3 tried to achieve with the X6 is just to take all of the

can really use your 360 camera for all of your shots. So if you want to record with either of

Both cameras also offer iLog color, so if you want to color grade your footage, but the X6 has that

I want to show you some comparisons of low light footage between these two cameras because that

better. As you can see in this comparison here, you can really zoom in a lot closer on your shots

caption_lines.text: The Insta360 X6 is here. And this clip was created automatically by the camera and the app.
No reframing, no editing – Zero Edit – one of the X6’s particular strengths. And the result is good,
significantly better than with previous tools. The X6 features three different automated editing
functions. I’ll show you how they work a little later. But apart from that, what else is new with
the X6, and just how good is the camera really? To find out, I compared the X6 to the best 360
cameras currently available. The X5 and the DJI Osmo360. The Osmo360 2 is due to be released soon,
but only in China. There is no information yet regarding an international release, and
a launch in the US is unlikely – the X5 and the Osmo360 are therefore currently the best cameras
for comparison.There are 10 categories that are important for the quality of a 360 camera. Take
a close look at all the categories, because there are a few interesting surprises. At the end, I’ll
tell you whether I think an upgrade makes sense and what special offers are currently available.
The X6 was provided to me by Insta360 for testing purposes, but this video does not
include any additional paid sponsorship! For the first time in a long while, Insta360
has completely redesigned the body of its 360 camera with the X6. The X6 no longer has that very
elongated shape. It’s slightly wider than the X5, but significantly shorter. In terms of form alone,
it’s a compromise between the X5 and the Osmo360. It still works well with a selfie stick, and the
slightly shorter form factor is better suited for mounting on a helmet or chest mount. In terms of
volume, it’s about the same size as the Osmo360 and slightly smaller than the X5. At 195 grams,
it weighs slightly more than the Osmo360 and just a bit less than the X5. Especially when
compared to the Osmo360, the X6 has a few key advantages. It features a significantly larger,
high-quality OLED-display. The X5’s display is similar in size, but its vertical format makes
it less suitable for single-lens shots. To make room for the X6’s large OLED display, the physical
buttons were moved to the side. In their place, two virtual buttons were added at the bottom
edge. Similar to modern smartphones, they provide haptic feedback when pressed. If needed, you can
even turn the entire screen into a record button. The display and camera feel very high-quality,
and the virtual buttons work very well—so well, in fact, that I hardly ever used the physical buttons
during my test recordings. Of course, that will be different in the winter when wearing gloves. And,
of course, the lens can be replaced on your own. Similar to the X5, there’s a Lens Replacement Kit
that lets you replace a damaged lens on your own. And that’s important: even though Insta360 says
the lenses have been reinforced and are supposed to be significantly less prone to scratches,
the protruding lenses are still a weak point of a 360 camera, since they can be easily damaged.
What I also like is that replacing a lens is now much easier than on the X5. And the lenses are
certainly one of the Osmo360’s biggest weaknesses in this comparison. On the one hand, you can’t
replace them yourself; you have to send the camera in if they’re damaged. On the other hand, the Osmo
360’s lenses can fog up, for example when there are extreme temperature differences, such as when
used in water. I also ran a similar test with the X6, and unlike the Osmo 360, it doesn’t fog up.
Incidentally, the X6 is waterproof to a depth of up to 20 metres without an additional dive case.
That’s more than the X5 or the Osmo360, which is only waterproof to a depth of 10 metres.
It all looks good—smaller, very well-built, a high-quality display. But ultimately,
what matters most is the image quality and how the footage looks.
Whenever a new camera is released, there’s always discussion about sponsored reviews. For me,
the solution is quite simple: I’ll explain the key differences to you and show you several
longer comparison clips that are unedited except for reframing. This way, you’ll be
able to form your own independent opinion. The X6 features two all-new 1/1.1-inch
sensors and improved chips. The new sensors are completely new square Sony sensors,
designed specifically for Insta360. At 1/1.1 inches, the new sensors are the
same size as those in the Osmo360 and larger than the X5’s sensors, which measure 1/1.28 inches.
When we compare the footage from the X6 with that from the X5, only minor differences are noticeable
at first glance. Both clips were reframed using the Field of View Mega. Interestingly,
the X5’s field of view is slightly wider. But there are a few other interesting differences.
The colors differ slightly. Especially here in the shots of this mountain meadow, the
X6’s colors appear more natural—they more closely match reality—the meadow is greener in reality,
just as it appears on the X6, and does not have the orange tones of the X5. Here’s a comparison
shot I took with an iPhone. But that’s perhaps the most noticeable difference in the colors. Much
greater and more significant are the differences in dynamic range. Compared to the X5, the X6 has a
clearly improved dynamic range, and highlights are preserved much better. You can see that,
for example, here in the background with the sun. And even more so in this shot here in the office.
You can clearly see how the details in the window are more blown out on the X5. Or in this example
with the castle. And there’s something else that stands out here. In some cases, the X5
shows unsightly blue lens flares. That’s not the case with the X6. In my opinion, the X6 comes
with very high-quality lenses, and I’ve actually never noticed any unsightly lens flares, even when
shooting against the sun. For me personally, this is one of the most important improvements in image
quality on the X6. By the way, there are no longer any settings for Adaptive Tone or HDR on the X6.
I see hardly any differences when it comes to detail—here’s a comparison at 400%. Both shots
show a similar level of detail. How does it compare to the Osmo360? Compared to the X5,
the Osmo360 produces shots with slightly less saturation. For these comparison shots,
I also used the standard field of view on both cameras. And these comparison shots don’t look all
that different either. It’s interesting that the Osmo360 often uses more magenta tones than the X6.
That wasn’t always the case in comparisons between DJI and Insta360 cameras. You can also see that in
this shot of the meadow on the mountain. The X6’s shot renders the meadow significantly greener than
the Osmo360’s. Sometimes, when shooting against the light, the Osmo360 tends to underexpose the
shot slightly. This makes the subject appear somewhat underexposed, as in this shot here. But

here in the office, the X6 performs only slightly better. The black T-shirt shows slightly more
detail in the X6’s shot, and the highlights are also preserved slightly better. Similar to the X5,
the Osmo360 can also have issues with lens flares in certain situations—and in this comparison,
you can see that the X6 handles lens flares significantly better than the Osmo360.
There’s one important topic we haven’t even touched on yet: Just like the Osmo360, the X6
can shoot in 8K at up to 50 frames per second. The X5 offers a maximum frame rate of 30 frames per
second in 8K. This is a significant upgrade, especially for those who prefer a slightly
smoother, more natural look. On the other hand, I’m a bit disappointed with the 360 slow-motion
footage. The X6 shoots in 4K at up to 100 frames per second, just like the Osmo360. The X5 is the
only one of the three cameras capable of shooting in 4K at 120 frames per second. On top of that,
I find that the X6’s image quality in 4K100 isn’t optimal, and that the X5, in particular, produces
better slow-motion footage in 4K. We’ll see that, fortunately, when it comes to slow motion, the X6
has a significant advantage in Single Lens mode. And the X6 has another feature that’s been long
overdue for Insta360. It supports 10-bit Log recording, even in 8K. The X5 does have a LOG
color profile, but only in 8-bit. Furthermore, the X5’s LOG profile isn’t available in 8K—only
in 5.7K. The Osmo360, on the other hand, also features a 10-bit Log profile that lets you
shoot in 8K. However, this is D-LOG M, and as you can see here, D-LOG M is nowhere near as flat as
the X6’s new Log profile. As a result, the dynamic range of the X6’s Log profile is better than that
of D-LOG M on the Osmo360. I converted these two clips using the manufacturers’ LUTs, and

But the X6 has another important advantage when it comes to color profiles. It’s the first 360 camera
capable of capturing 8K 360 footage in 10-bit HDR Dolby Vision. This means footage where,

you’ll need an HDR-capable display, such as the screen of a modern smartphone or a modern TV. As

looks more realistic. As my YouTube review isn’t an HDR video, I can’t show the full
dynamic range. But I get the impression that HDR videos sometimes look a bit overexposed,
even when viewed on a smartphone. Insta360 could do with making some improvements in this area.
You can reframe your 360 Dolby Vision video as usual and export it as an HDR Dolby Vision video.
This is a great feature for anyone who frequently watches their videos on a smartphone or TV.
The X6 has also made slight improvements in low-light performance. The X6 is the
best 360 camera to date for shooting in low light. Similar to the X5 and the Osmo 360,
it has its own dedicated shooting mode for use in low light. However,
the difference compared to the X5 isn’t that big. Especially considering the size of its sensor,
the X5 already takes very good shots in low light. It’s also extremely dark here. Actually,
you shouldn’t really be filming in such lighting conditions. But this scenario is
simply better suited for comparison shots and to better highlight the differences. As I said,
the difference compared to the X5’s footage really isn’t that big. The X6’s footage has slightly less
image noise and is a bit sharper. And here, too, you can see that the issues with lens flares have
been resolved. The same applies when compared to the Osmo360. The Osmo360’s footage is darker and
lacks some detail. As mentioned at the beginning, the Osmo360 has sensors the same size as the X6.
This means that the performance of the Pure Video mode is simply the deciding factor,

Interestingly, the differences in Single Lens mode are perhaps greater overall than in 360
mode. The X6 clearly performs better here. This is true both when compared to the Osmo360 and
when compared to the X5. The colors in the X6’s recordings look better, and they also show more
detail. And that brings us to a topic where the X6 has made great progress: the single-lens mode.
As we’ve just seen, the X6 clearly performs best in low-light conditions among all three cameras
in Single Lens mode. But that’s not the only improvement Insta360 has made in Single Lens
mode. All three cameras can capture flat footage with just one lens, which you no longer need to
reframe. And just like the Osmo360, the X6 can now also capture flat footage in 5K at up to 60 frames

That’s really cool – the footage in Single Lens mode looks good, but I’ve also noticed that the
Osmo 360 and the X5 apply more HDR processing. The highlights can blow out a bit more quickly
on the X6 in Single Lens mode. I don’t know if that might change with a future firmware update.
what I’m really excited about is that with the X6 in Single Lens mode, you can now also shoot
slow-motion footage in 4K at up to 120 frames per second. This is also possible with the Osmo 360,
but only in the extremely wide ‘Boost’ mode. With the X6, 4K120 is available in Single
Lens mode regardless of the field of view. This means the X6 is increasingly capable of
replacing a traditional action camera. High-quality slow-motion footage has
been one of the few remaining exclusive features of a standard action camera.
Of course, all three cameras still have several other shooting modes, such as for time-lapses
or hyperlapses. Just like the Osmo360, the X6 can take 360 photos with up to 120 megapixels.
I’ve done a comparison of a few photos here in the office, as many people are interested in
indoor 360° photos. This is a heavily cropped version of the photos. Unlike the Osmo360,
the X6 has a significantly higher dynamic range, also because it features an HDR mode. The level
of detail is also slightly better than on the Osmo360. Compared to the X5, there’s a
noticeable improvement in detail, partly because the X5’s photo has significantly fewer megapixels.
There have also been improvements to the Bullet Time mode. The Bullet Time mode is
now available for the first time in 8K at up to 100 frames per second. But I find
the Instaframe mode—which is exclusive to the X6 and X5—much more interesting. In Instaframe mode,
you can select a subject and track it directly in the camera, much like you would with a gimbal
camera. You’ll then get a perfectly reframed flat clip in 4K with the “Invisible Selfie
Stick” effect. No more editing required. The tracking and reframing are therefore performed
directly in the camera. If needed, you can also simultaneously record a 360 backup clip in 8K,
which you can reframe yourself—just in case you’re not satisfied with the flat clip.
Simultaneous recording in 4K and 8K—that’s not possible with the X5. When recording a
flat clip and a 360 clip at the same time, the resolution on the X5 must be reduced to 1080.
And that brings us to a topic that sets the X6 and Insta360 apart. The goal is to increasingly
relieve users of the need to edit and reframe their footage. After all, reframing is still
considered the biggest drawback of a 360 camera. To take the reframing off the user’s hands, the X6
supports a new, completely revamped Autoedit feature in the app. You select a few clips,
and the app does the rest. Until now, the results were rather average. That has now actually been
improved. By the way, the intro clip was created using the new Auto Edit feature.
But there are two more new features. With the new AI Director feature,
the X6 analyzes all clips recorded that day at the end of the day and while charging,
identifies highlights, and automatically transfers a custom-generated daily vlog to
your smartphone—all fully automatically—you don’t actually have to do anything except activate the
feature. Everything runs on the camera and app. No upload to the cloud is required for this feature.
With AI Director, you don’t even have to select the clips yourself. This feature automatically
compiles a montage of some of the best shots of the day, which you can share straight away.
In contrast, the new cloud features, Moments & Moments Pro, which work in conjunction with Google
Gemini, are quite different. After you’ve uploaded your clips to the cloud, Moments Pro becomes a
kind of personal editor. The clips are analyzed, and various editing schemes are suggested. You
can then select different tags or protagonists and start the edit. This process takes place entirely
in the cloud, and you’ll be notified as soon as the video is ready. The feature is interesting and
works well, but there’s a catch—you’ll naturally need a cloud subscription to take advantage of it.
depending on the keyword, it can also pick out key scenes from older,
perhaps even forgotten, recordings. All three features represent an upgrade
to the previous AutoEdit function. Generally speaking, in my opinion, it’s not about getting
the best possible result from your footage. Rather, it’s about getting a good montage of
your footage quickly and easily, without having to do the editing yourself if you don’t feel
like it. And the results can be really cool! But that isn’t a feature exclusive to the X6.
all the new automated editing features will also be available for the X5. If you’d like to find
out more about the new Autoedit features, have a look at my tutorial on the subject.
I’ll include a link to it in the description. With all these new features and the smaller
form factor, the question of recording time naturally arises. So how long can the X6 shoot,
and are there any overheating issues? I ran a test here in the office at 8K30 at
a warm 26 degrees Celsius and without any airflow. Under these unfavorable conditions, there were no
overheating issues whatsoever, and the X6 was able to shoot for an incredible 2 hours and 38 minutes.
That’s 1 hour and 10 minutes longer than the Osmo360 and the X5. Only the X5 had overheating
issues under these conditions and shut down after 56 minutes due to overheating. Of course,
it’s worth noting that in real-world use and with airflow, none of the three cameras will have
overheating problems. For most people, overheating will therefore remain more of a theoretical issue.
But Insta360 has gotten everything right this time when it comes to overheating and battery life.
To capture shots like this one or this underwater shot, a 360 camera requires
very specific accessories. And in this regard, not only the X6 but also the X5 have a major—if
not decisive—advantage. It’s true that all sticks and mounts are compatible with all 360
cameras. But Insta360 is the only manufacturer so far to offer an Invisible Dive case for its
360 cameras. And only with such a dive case can you take 360° shots underwater, since underwater
shots place entirely different demands on lens stitching. Unfortunately, the Dive Case for

here. But a Dive Case for the X6 will be available soon. However, a dive case is now also available
for the X6. Apart from that, there are several remote controls, ND filters and other special
mounts and accessories available for the X6. And have you seen this: the Luna Ultra’s POV
Head Tracker? It’s worn like a headset and is also compatible with the X6. When using the
Instframe mode, The framing automatically adjusts to the movements of your head.
Personally, I wouldn't want to do without the DiveCase. For me personally,
the lack of an Invisible Dive Case is one of the Osmo360’s major weaknesses
I know that many users aren't particularly interested in audio quality. But Insta360 has been
constantly working to further improve the audio quality of its cameras—and the X6 is no exception.
The X6 features a new Windproof 360 microphone. The camera has microphone openings on all sides
that are protected from the wind. And of course, the X6 also includes the excellent
Voice Enhancement mode, which effectively filters out background noise. But of course,
for even better audio quality, there are external microphones available for all
three cameras. The best choice for the X6 is definitely the relatively new Mic Pro.
What else is important? What other differences are there between the three cameras? The X6 also
comes with a very special feature: 3D Spatial Capture. Put simply, this is a technique that
creates a 3D model from a video or photo – a 3D model within which you can move around freely.

a house that you can explore virtually and freely. For many people, this is certainly a very cool
feature. Unfortunately, 3D Spatial Capture is not available in the US at launch for technical
reasons. However, this is set to change. And for me, very important:
Unlike the X5, the X6 finally has internal storage. At 47 gigabytes, it’s only about
half as much as the Osmo 360, but it’s enough in case you forget your SD card. And, of course,
the apps are important, too. Especially when compared to other manufacturers, the Insta360 apps
are still the best in terms of feature set. This applies to both the smartphone app and the desktop
app. That said, you can of course also reframe your clips quite well with the DJI Mimo app.
I think the X6 has turned out to be a fantastic camera that gets almost everything right. And
the new AutoEdit features and 3D Spatial Capture expand the functionality of a 360-degree camera.
Of course, that comes at a price. The Insta360 X6 starts at $699 in the U.S. and at €699 in Europe.

starting at $550 or €590 in Europe. The Osmo360 is similarly priced, but you can find it cheaper from
third-party retailers like Amazon. You’ll find links to all three cameras in the description
below. If you use the link for the X6, You'll also receive an exclusive creator gift pack. It's

applies to DJI and GoPro cameras as well. I’ll include a link to this in the description too.
So what would I recommend? In my opinion, the X6 has turned out to be a perfect 360 camera. It has
hardly any flaws, and aside from slow-motion in 360 mode, there’s hardly anything more you could
ask for right now. I really like the new lenses and the fact that all the lens flare issues have
been fixed. The new automated editing options are cool, too. It’s basically a flawless camera,
though it doesn’t have any absolutely standout killer features. If you’re buying a new camera

caption_lines.text: GoPro's adhesive mounts are arguably the most versatile option for mounting your GoPro to
most surfaces that more conventional mounts can't handle.
Follow these very simple steps for optimal attachment and your mount will be able to
stand up to the most extreme environments.
I'll be demonstrating the process on my brand new Smith Vantage helmet, but the same steps
apply to any surface you plan on attaching to.
You will need a few things; a flat or curved GoPro adhesive mount (depending on how flat
or curved your surface is), the GoPro quick release buckle and white rubber anti-vibration
locking plug, some isopropyl rubbing alcohol (available in any pharmacy or convenience
store), measuring tape and a pencil (for finding and marking the center line) and some sort
of clamping tool.
The first step, is to determine where you want to attach the adhesive mount.
The options on a helmet are endless, but some recommended points are front and center, top
center or on one of the sides.
I'm going to be mounting mine front and center, so I can capture forward-facing point of view
footage, as well as self portrait type footage.
At this point, you need to decide whether to use a flat or curved adhesive mount.
Taking into account the curve of the helmet - it looks like the curved one will work best
in this situation.
I want my GoPro to be perfectly centered to minimize adjustments in post production, so
I need to find a center line to follow.
To do this, find two symmetrical points that are equally spaced apart (in this case the
two front vents).
Measure the distance between the points, and make a mark exactly half way between them.
Always, make sure to double check your work to avoid a crooked mount.
Now that we have our first point, we need to make another one to get a straight line.
Find another two symmetrical points (in this case the two vents that are on top of the
helmet), and make another mark.
Now use the tape measure or other straight edge to connect the two lines - this is your
center line.
The GoPro adhesive mounts use 3M VHB adhesive tape, and 3M has a pretty long instruction
manual on proper surface preparation.
To put it simply, the surface must be completely clean and free of any dirts or oils.
For most applications, they recommend using a 50:50 mixture of isopropyl alcohol and water.
Mix these two together, apply it to some sort of cloth or towel and rub the surface to prep
it for adhesion.
You might rub off some of your center line in the process, but that's why I made it longer
than I needed.
Now grab your adhesive mount, peel off its backing and slowly apply it while aligning
its' center with your center line.
Once you are happy with its' placement, apply as much pressure as you can with your hands.
The strength of the bond takes up to 72 hours to reach 100% of its potential, and maintaining
pressure on it will aid that process.
So for optimal adhesion, you can use some c-clamps, spring clamps or some sort of other
clamp to sustain pressure on it for an extended period of time.
This step is not absolutely necessary, but I like to take all the precautions possible
when it comes to these pricey little cameras.
If this video helped you avoid a sticky situation with your adhesive GoPro mounts, give me a
thumbs up, share it with your friends and subscribe for more GoPro tips and DIYs!

JOBY GorillaPod Action GoPro Tripod (JB01300) Review & Unboxing | GoPro Tips & Tricks

caption_lines.text: Joby has recently released their newest iteration of it's famous GorillaPod tripod - the Action
Series of tripods and mounts.
The GorillaPod Action tripod is specifically designed to work with the GoPro and other
action cameras.
The GorillaPod Action Tripod comes complete with an aluminum ballhead, a quick-release
clip with the standard GoPro mount and a standard 1/4"-20 tripod adapter.
The Action Tripod is about 10" long, making it about 1.5x times longer than the GorillaPod
Original, and about the same length as the GorillaPod SLR-Zoom - with significantly thinner
legs.
Although the Original is more compact, the longer legs of the Action give it more versatility
when reaching around whatever object you are mounting it to, providing a better hold and
ultimately securing your camera from loss or damage.
The thickness of the legs makes them slightly less maneuverable than the Original, but this,
too, ensures a better hold in the often unpredictable environment of action photography.
Arguably, the best feature of this tripod, is the integrated aluminum ballhead - giving
you the flexibility to 360 degree panning and 90 degree tilting.
The rubberized tightening knob, makes panning and tilting a breeze.
A bubble level is provided to give you level shots even without an LCD BacPac or the iPhone
app for preview.
Adjusting the ballhead truly gives you complete control to frame the perfect shot - every
time.
Included in the box is a quick-release clip with a standard 1/4"-20 tripod adapter, allowing
you to mount virtually any compact camera.
You simply screw it into your camera, slide it on to the GorillaPod's shoe and when you're
done - press the release button and slide it out.
The GorillaPod Action Tripod also comes with a quick-release mount specifically for the
GoPro.
Just connect your GoPro with a standard thumbscrew, slide it into the Action Tripod and you're
good to go.
Disconnecting works exactly the same way - with the press of the release button.
Now you may be asking yourself - "but GoPro already has a quick-release system, why would
GorillaPod create their own?"
This is a good point, but GoPro's system is bulkier and a lot of people have more cameras
than just a GoPro.
As an owner of several different cameras myself, I see the versatility of GorillaPod's quick-release
system as a plus.
If you wan't to use GoPro's quick-release system instead, don't worry - I have the perfect
solution for you.
With GoPro's new tripod mount, you get a GoPro quick-release 1/4"-20 tripod mount adapter.
Screw this onto GorillaPods 1/4"-20 tripod mount, and now you can easily switch from
mount to mount.
GorillaPod's are meant to be mounted on any object that they can wrap their legs around,
and the Action Tripod is no exception!
Due to it's versatility, the GorillaPod Action Tripod gets my approval - and I believe it
is an essential part of any amateur or professional GoPro users kit.

subscribe for more GoPro tips and DIYs!

clips.title: The Speed vs Effort Myth: How to Ride Fast With Less Effort

caption_lines.text: I remember in my early life on the
track, as I started to go faster, the
mental strain and the amount of effort
it took physically became more and more
difficult. And at the time, I felt this
was normal. You're going faster, which
means your brain and body is working
harder to deal with the speed. But what
I eventually came to realize is that
while speed equals more effort is true
to some degree, there's actually a lot
less correlation between speed and
effort than you might think, which is
exactly what we're going to talk about
today. I'm going to share the main
traits and skills that determine how
difficult riding really feels and how
improving them can actually help you
ride faster with less effort. Some will
be longer-term improvements, but others
will benefit you almost immediately. And
while this is mostly going to be in the
context of the track, I have found that
a lot of this applies to my road riding,
too. So, if you generally want to know
how riding can feel easier, stick
around. All right, so let's quickly get
this one out of the way that I know most
people don't want to talk about, and
that's your fitness levels.
If we go to the extreme ends of this,
top MotoGP riders are among the fittest
athletes on the planet. They need high
levels of strength and stamina to deal
with everything that that level of
riding throws at them. Now, you
definitely don't need to have those
fitness levels to ride fast and enjoy
riding. And this is clear when you start
to get a few rungs down on the
motorcycle racing ladder, where you find
riders that are still very fast by 99.9%
of people's standards, but they don't
look like the MotoGP elite. Having said
that, the simple fact is that the fitter
and stronger you are, the easier you're
going to find it to ride because your
body doesn't have to work as hard to do
what you're asking it to do. And where
this usually shows up is not so much in
speed over one or two laps, but how long
a rider can ride at that pace, and also
how tired they feel towards the end of a
day's riding. Honestly, unless you
genuinely want to, I wouldn't suggest
anyone needs to be in peak physical
fitness, but even just a basic level of
strength and stamina will make a
difference to how you feel during and
after your rides. Not to mention it just
means you're generally healthier, which
is only a good thing in my book. But I
appreciate that this is one area that
can take time to really improve.
However, these next few will help you
much quicker. The first is how you're
approaching the corner and using the
brakes. I fell into the same trap as
many other riders in thinking that the
way to go faster was to brake as late as
I could and use them as little as
possible. And on paper it makes sense.
If I'm braking very late, it means I'm
accelerating for longer down the
straight, slowing down for less time,
and carrying more speed into the
corners. But while many newer riders
would benefit from braking later and
using more braking potential, past a
certain point it can actually make
things harder. Because if you're already
braking to a decent level, trying to
brake a bike length or two later, it may
save you fractions of time at the end of
the straight, but you'll probably lose
that and more on the other side of the
braking zone and as you move into corner
entry. Because being in maximum attack
mode like this often leads to overwhelm
and over braking. And to bring it back
into the context of this video, it just
makes riding feel an awful lot harder
physically and mentally. By going back
to a more sensible braking point, which
reduces the mental and physical
bombardment, it not only means you can
ride in a calmer state, but you'll
probably see bigger benefits in terms of
speed, too. All while putting in less
physical effort. Now, there is nuance
here and this will be more important in
some corners than others, particularly
in medium to high speed corners where
you spend more time in them because
corner speed is just more important
there. The biggest indicator that this
is a problem for you is where you have
corners where you feel like you're
braking very late and using a lot of
braking potential, but you're still
going too slow into and through that
corner. This shows you're probably
attacking those corners a little too
much and if you have a few of them over

a little earlier and less aggressively,
