clips.title: Why You Can’t Get Your Knee Down (and how to fix it)

caption_lines.text: There are many noteworthy milestones in
the life of a motorcyclist, whether it's
getting a license, a big bike upgrade,
or the first time you go tarmac surfing.
But, there are very few that are as
sought after or well remembered as
getting your knee down, particularly if
you're a biker of the sporty variety.
And yes, I know you can argue that it's
pretty arbitrary and doesn't make you a
better rider. But, it is still something
many riders want to achieve, something
they will struggle with, and something
that's fondly remembered after it
happens, which was exactly the case for
me. After being on the track for 18
months, I was going pretty well in the
advanced group, but I still hadn't got
my knee down, and I was getting
increasingly frustrated by it. But, one
day at Snetterton in 2011 during a
coaching session with Neil Hodgson, it
finally happened. I experienced the
distinct but faintest touch of my knee
slider scraping the track, something
that left me grinning from ear to ear
while I sat there gently caressing the
abrasion of my slider back in the
paddock. So, trust me when I say that I
understand the frustration of not being
able to do it, along with the relief and
pleasure of finally achieving this
riding milestone. So, we're going to go
through all the main reasons why riders
struggle with it, because it's more than
just body position, and the best ways to
overcome them so that you can finally
get there for yourself. Now, even though
I say it's not just body position, that
is where we're going to start, focusing
on the main mistakes with it that make
it getting your knee down that much
harder. So, in simple terms, the peg is
typically the first thing to touch down
as the bike reaches maximum lean. So, as
long as your knee is sticking out
further than that as it relates to the
contact patch, then it means your knee
should always touch the ground first.
So, getting into that position is the
first goal. But, riders do make that
more difficult in a number of ways. The
first is, sorry to say, just having
short legs, simply because they won't
stick out as far. Now, it doesn't mean
that knee down is impossible, but it
does mean you need to get these next
pieces right in order to give yourself
the best chance.
Things like making sure you're sliding
off the seat enough with one half to one
whole cheek usually being enough, making
sure your heel is turned in so that your
toes are pointing out, and making sure
your body is facing slightly into the
turn rather than being crossed up and
pointing away from it. Something that
forces your knee forward to the front of
the bike as opposed to out to the side.
Fixing these things will help open up
your hips and extend your knee further
out. But you also need to be relaxed
enough to actually open your hips like
this, and that's why having the proper
lower body support is important here. If
that support is poor, you're going to
have to rely on your arms, typically
meaning your head will drift back into
the center creating that same crossed up
position. But you may also find that you
have a little too much strain on your
legs, too, making it difficult to relax
and open up your hips as needed. Now,
you're always going to have a good deal
of weight on that inside peg because the
majority of your mass is on top of it.
But good body position and anchoring
will mean it just doesn't become
excessive, making sticking that knee out
that much easier.
Okay, so body position is the first box
to tick. Ultimately, making sure your
knee is sticking out far enough and
you're actually comfortable doing it.
But in my experience, that's the easiest
bit to get right with these next two
being significantly harder. One of those
being the psychological barriers. Okay,
so your knee is sticking out far enough,
but if you aren't leaning the bike
enough, then outside of parting company
with it, your knee is never going to
touch the ground. And one of the main
factors that prevent riders doing that
is the fear they have around it. And for
me, this typically two things behind the
fear of leaning. The rider doesn't trust
the equipment under them, or they don't
trust themselves and their ability to
not crash. They don't trust what's under
them because they aren't really sure
what the bike and tires can handle. Is
it safe to lean that far? Will the tires
be okay if I do? How do I know if the
tires are going to let go? And no matter
how much a rider wants to lean further,
with those questions swirling around in
their heads, it's all too easy to just
stay in their comfort zone. One of the
very best ways to build confidence in
what's under you is to simply look at
other riders who are using the same
equipment as you. If you can see riders
going much faster with the bike cranked
right over and then knee on the deck
with the similar machinery and tires,
that in itself is proof that they are
capable. Also, don't be afraid to
upgrade to stickier rubber if your tires
aren't giving you confidence. Now, that
doesn't mean going out and buying the
stickiest race rubber you can, but even
moving from, say, a sports touring tire
to a modern track day tire, that extra
feeling of grip could make all the
difference. But like I said, getting
confidence in what's under you is just
the first part. The second is having
confidence in yourself and your own
ability. If you don't know or understand
good fundamental skill and what you
should be doing with the controls at any
given moment, it can make it difficult
to push to those high lean angles
because you just aren't sure you're
doing things correctly. By taking time
to learn and improve your fundamental
skill, you start to develop confidence
purely through knowing that you are in
fact doing the right things. This helps
reduce the fear of things suddenly going
wrong because you now have confidence in
yourself as well as your ability to
avoid crashing. However, while knowing
that is important, I know from personal
experience that you're not just going to
suddenly blast past your riding barriers
just because you know that. So, the way
to truly chip away and eventually
overcome them is by putting yourself in
a position to tackle them properly,
leading us onto the final change riders
need to make, which is their cornering
approach. Specifically in the context of
trying to break these barriers and
finally reaching knee down. But before
we get to that, really quickly, if you
are a rider trying to break these
barriers and you're trying to reach high
levels on the track, we're actually
running a free 4-day online workshop
that helps you do exactly that. Over 4
days, you'll learn how the best riders
consistently make progress by finding
weaknesses, creating plans to tackle
them, and then heading out there in the
right way to make real progress. To join
us, there's a link in the description
and in the top pinned comment. Riders
really love this workshop, so I'm
excited for you to jump in and get
something from it, too. All right, so
most riders instinctively know that they
need to lean the bike more and that they
need more speed going into corners to do
it. But this often leads them to being
more aggressive and trying to brake
later and force the speed into corners,
which funnily enough has the complete
opposite effect of stripping speed they
need through over-braking while taking
away the calmness and composure we
actually need.
But riders on the other end of the scale
will struggle, too. If they're way too
tentative and they roll off a long way
from the corner while barely using any
brakes, that's going to make entering
corners with more speed difficult, too.
So in my experience, the best approach
is something in the middle while also
doing it on corners that lend themselves
well to breaking this tricky barrier.
For me, that means slightly longer
medium-speed corners that require a fair
bit of braking, but not high levels of
braking, like you would going into a
hairpin after a straight, for example.
Palmer at Snetterton is a perfect
example of a great corner to practice
on. It's a medium-speed corner where you
spend a fair bit of time in it. This
means you have more time to focus on
your lean angle and what you're doing
with your knee. And because you don't
need to use hard brakes because the
corner before is a slow hairpin, it's
easier to stay calm and be more
deliberate with your braking effort,
which is the key for rolling more speed
into the corner. And by braking effort
being the key, that doesn't mean
breaking as late as possible and
attacking the corner, but instead
working to release the lever a little
earlier to incrementally increase entry
speed. Because with everything else
remaining the same, if you release the
brake lever quicker and earlier towards
the end of your braking effort, you're
naturally going to roll more speed into
that corner. This is how we want to
increase our corner speed when working
on this kind of barrier. So, that's the
first step, putting yourself in the best
position to roll more speed in. Then
comes the hard part, actually leaning.
If you did in fact roll more speed into
the corner, you'll likely feel a mild
sense of panic that you're going too
fast. That's completely normal. Keep
your eyes up and ahead to show yourself
the space is there and it shouldn't get
too out of control. At this point,
you'll be counter steering and leaning
into the corner. And what will probably
happen is you'll bump up against your
lean angle barrier again. That's okay.
With it being a longer corner, you have
time to notice it and then to tell
yourself to lean that little bit more.
Gently push on the inside bar while
remaining off the throttle or at most
neutral throttle and the bike will lean
more. And at this point, don't be afraid
to really stick your knee out.
Ordinarily, you don't want to strain to
do this, but if it means getting that
first touch, then that's fine. Now, if
you didn't get it down, don't worry. You
now know what the plan is. Release the
brake lever a little earlier again so
that you go a little faster into the
corner next time. But if you're at a
point where you feel like you're barely
breaking at all and still not going fast
enough, then you probably need to move
your initial breaking point closer to
the corner so that you're actually using
the brakes, regaining that adjustability
you need to do this. And this is all it
takes. Incrementally increase your speed
through your brake release while
practicing conscious counter steering to
increase lean angle bit by bit. If your
body is in the position we talked about
and your knee is sticking out far
enough, eventually, it will touch down.
And while this isn't necessarily the
perfect approach for going fast, what
we're doing here is isolating the
barrier that we're trying to overcome
and making it as easy as possible to
tackle it. And once you can do that
consistently on one corner, that
confidence will start to bleed into all
the other corners and you'll start
getting your knee down there as well. As
someone that took longer than most to
get that first knee down all those years
ago, I know how frustrating and
impossible it can feel at times. But
with a bit of conscious effort, it's
only a matter of time before you can get
there, too. And if you're anything like
me, it's still going to make you grin
like a woolly for many years to come.
Now, everything I've just shared with
you around this is stuff I wish I knew
when I got first started on the track,
but there's plenty more. And to see 21
other truths that I wish I knew when I
got started with motorcycles that I
think everyone should know, check out
this video here. Outside of that, thank
you so much for joining me for this one,
and I will see you in the next one. Take
care.

caption_lines.text: GoPro's adhesive mounts are arguably the most versatile option for mounting your GoPro to
most surfaces that more conventional mounts can't handle.
Follow these very simple steps for optimal attachment and your mount will be able to
stand up to the most extreme environments.
I'll be demonstrating the process on my brand new Smith Vantage helmet, but the same steps
apply to any surface you plan on attaching to.
You will need a few things; a flat or curved GoPro adhesive mount (depending on how flat
or curved your surface is), the GoPro quick release buckle and white rubber anti-vibration
locking plug, some isopropyl rubbing alcohol (available in any pharmacy or convenience
store), measuring tape and a pencil (for finding and marking the center line) and some sort
of clamping tool.
The first step, is to determine where you want to attach the adhesive mount.
The options on a helmet are endless, but some recommended points are front and center, top
center or on one of the sides.
I'm going to be mounting mine front and center, so I can capture forward-facing point of view
footage, as well as self portrait type footage.
At this point, you need to decide whether to use a flat or curved adhesive mount.
Taking into account the curve of the helmet - it looks like the curved one will work best
in this situation.
I want my GoPro to be perfectly centered to minimize adjustments in post production, so
I need to find a center line to follow.
To do this, find two symmetrical points that are equally spaced apart (in this case the
two front vents).
Measure the distance between the points, and make a mark exactly half way between them.
Always, make sure to double check your work to avoid a crooked mount.
Now that we have our first point, we need to make another one to get a straight line.
Find another two symmetrical points (in this case the two vents that are on top of the
helmet), and make another mark.
Now use the tape measure or other straight edge to connect the two lines - this is your
center line.
The GoPro adhesive mounts use 3M VHB adhesive tape, and 3M has a pretty long instruction
manual on proper surface preparation.
To put it simply, the surface must be completely clean and free of any dirts or oils.
For most applications, they recommend using a 50:50 mixture of isopropyl alcohol and water.
Mix these two together, apply it to some sort of cloth or towel and rub the surface to prep
it for adhesion.
You might rub off some of your center line in the process, but that's why I made it longer
than I needed.
Now grab your adhesive mount, peel off its backing and slowly apply it while aligning
its' center with your center line.
Once you are happy with its' placement, apply as much pressure as you can with your hands.
The strength of the bond takes up to 72 hours to reach 100% of its potential, and maintaining
pressure on it will aid that process.
So for optimal adhesion, you can use some c-clamps, spring clamps or some sort of other
clamp to sustain pressure on it for an extended period of time.
This step is not absolutely necessary, but I like to take all the precautions possible
when it comes to these pricey little cameras.
If this video helped you avoid a sticky situation with your adhesive GoPro mounts, give me a
thumbs up, share it with your friends and subscribe for more GoPro tips and DIYs!
